USWDS RenderbyOddball

Ask a question. Get a real government interface.

A chatbot answers in paragraphs. USWDS Render answers in a custom user interface.

The Challenge

"What Medicare Advantage plans are available in ZIP 97201?"

Ask a chatbot and you get what a chatbot gives you: paragraphs.

Prose is a bad container for an answer people have to act on.

Nothing lines up. Premiums, star ratings, and out-of-pocket caps are lost in a huge block of text.

Nothing to act on. No plan link, no next step — just text and an implied "go look it up somewhere else."

Nothing scales. Three plans is a long paragraph. Ten is a wall nobody finishes reading.

The Oddball Solution

Enter USWDS Render.

The question goes in. An interface comes back.

Same Question, Rendered

Three plans, side by side — each card built exactly the same way..

Not a custom layout. These are real components — the same ones Medicare.gov is built from.

How It Works

Three steps, every answer.

It calls tools, not memory. The question goes to an agent that resolves ZIP 97201 to Multnomah County, then searches plans actually offered in that county. The data is fetched, not recalled.

It emits a spec, not prose. The agent returns a JSON tree of component names and props — validated against a schema catalog before a single pixel renders. An unknown component never reaches the page.

{
  "root": "root",
  "elements": {
    "root": {
      "type": "Section",
      "children": ["status", "title", "intro", ...]
    },
    "status": { "type": "Alert", ... },
    ...
    "plan-1": {
      "type": "MedicarePlanCard",
      "props": {
        "planName": "Pioneer Advantage Choice (PPO)",
        "monthlyPremium": "$0/month",
        "starRating": "4.5 stars",
        "maxOutOfPocket": "$4,900"
      }
    },
    ...

The registry renders it. Each node maps to a real component and streams in as it arrives — drawn from the actual registry of real USWDS and CMS Design System components.

Why It Holds Up

The AI picks components. It doesn't invent them.

Patterns people already know. Users have met these components on every .gov site they've used.

Accessible by construction. Section 508 and WCAG work lives in the component, not in whatever the model wrote this time.

Fix it once, everywhere. Improve a component and every answer that uses it improves with it. Nothing to regenerate.

Consistent on the tenth run. Same question, same components, same layout.

Same flexibility as a chatbot — but the answer arrives as a reliable, accessible government interface.
